 Dakota Meyer describes poor barracks conditions as he reviews military housing
 Saturday, 7 November 2026, 12:46 
 Photo source: Fox News 
 Some U.S. troops have gone a year without hot water, while others sleep in their cars to escape barracks without air conditioning, Medal of Honor recipient Dakota Meyer says. 
 Meyer, a senior adviser to the Pentagon’s Barracks Task Force, has visited more than eight Army, Navy, Air Force and Marine Corps installations since War Secretary Pete Hegseth assigned him to address decades of neglect. He plans to visit 30 before the end of the year. In an interview with Fox News Digital on Thursday, Meyer said only a couple of the barracks he had seen were in good condition.
 This is reported by Fox News .
 At one installation, Meyer asked a 19-year-old service member what she would change if she could “wave a magic wand.” Her answer was a hot shower, he said: “It’s absolutely heartbreaking.”
 Advertisement 
 A 2023 Government Accountability Office investigation found serious health and safety hazards in barracks. It also found that the Defense Department lacked reliable information about their condition, could not determine how much of its facilities spending went toward them and provided insufficient oversight. Congress and the military services have since committed billions of dollars to improvements, but problems persist: 12 of the GAO’s 31 recommendations remained outstanding as of 2026.
 Hegseth has sought to centralize the work under a department-wide task force and speed up improvements. Meyer said the secretary expects him to act, not just identify problems: “He expects me to fix it,” Meyer said. “And that’s exactly what we’re going to do.” Meyer said he had asked Hegseth to give the task force an “authoritative role,” including the ability to make decisions and direct where funding goes and how quickly it reaches service members.
 Meyer said the problem involves funding shortfalls, continuing resolutions and years of deferred maintenance, as well as contracting rules and bureaucracy that can delay repairs. A separate watchdog review found a $285 billion maintenance backlog across the Pentagon’s broader military facilities portfolio. Meyer also pointed to Congress’ failure to pass full-year defense appropriations for fiscal 2027. The Pentagon is operating under a continuing resolution through Dec. 11, which generally funds ongoing programs at prior-year rates while lawmakers negotiate a broader spending package.
 Meyer said progress should be measured by whether troops see better living conditions, not only by how much money has been obligated or put under contract. He said service members have asked for hot showers, places to wash clothes, doors that lock, mold-free rooms and light bulbs. He added that many installation commanders want to improve conditions but lack the ability to do so, calling the issue “a multidimensional problem” that is “complex.”
 Meyer criticized previous Pentagon leadership, saying barracks had not been a priority despite years of investment and reform efforts. He said Hegseth had made the issue a personal priority. Meyer has said he would take responsibility if the barracks are not fixed. Asked what “fixed” would look like, he said: “People are living in places that I would be okay for my daughters living in.”
